m1-t1.introduction: Picture a local café as a connected system: people discover it, decide to try it and find a reason to come back. Each channel earns its place by doing a different job.

sections.title: The attract → convert → keep loop
sections.explanation: A post is an activity. Marketing connects that activity to a customer action, then uses the result to improve the next round.

items.label: Attract
items.detail: A nearby search or useful reel introduces the café.

items.label: Convert
items.detail: A clear menu and ordering path turn interest into an order.

items.label: Keep
items.detail: An opted-in breakfast update gives regulars a reason to return.

items.label: Measure
items.detail: Count enquiries, orders and repeat visits, then adjust.

sections.takeaway: Judge the system by useful customer actions, not how much content it produces.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. The definition that matters: attract, convert, keep — measurably

sections.title: Three media engines, one business
sections.explanation: Owned, earned and paid media differ in control, trust and cost. They are complements, not three competing strategies.

items.label: Owned
items.detail: Website and permission-based list: build a reusable relationship.

items.label: Earned
items.detail: Independent reviews and mentions: other people supply proof.

items.label: Paid
items.detail: Ads and sponsored placements: buy distribution, then stop paying when it stops helping.

sections.takeaway: A platform-hosted profile is not fully under your control; a permission-based contact list is still subject to privacy and provider rules.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. Owned, earned and paid — the three kinds of media

sections.title: Give every channel a job
sections.explanation: Instead of picking channels because they are popular, start with the job needed in the customer relationship.

items.label: Search
items.detail: Capture an existing question or nearby need.

items.label: Content
items.detail: Explain the offer and remove uncertainty.

items.label: Social
items.detail: Make the business familiar and support conversation.

items.label: Email / messaging
items.detail: Follow up with people who have chosen to hear from you.

items.label: Paid media
items.detail: Amplify a relevant message to an appropriate audience.

sections.takeaway: The same customer can move between several channels before ordering.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. The channels and their actual jobs

sections.title: Build the shop before announcing the sale
sections.explanation: Always-on assets make the business findable every day. A time-bound campaign adds urgency to an already usable customer experience.

items.label: Always-on foundation
items.detail: Accurate listing, helpful pages, working order link and regular replies.

items.label: Campaign burst
items.detail: A two-week festival offer with a goal, dates and a measurement plan.

sections.takeaway: Do not pay to send people to a broken page or an unanswered inbox.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Is an Instagram posting schedule a complete marketing strategy?
checkpoint.answer: No. Name the audience and business goal, the action each channel supports, and the way you will measure orders or another useful outcome.

m1-t2.introduction: Follow one customer from discovery to a repeat purchase, then put numbers on the journey. Use the interactive funnel to see why fixing a leak can beat buying more traffic.

sections.title: Five stages, five customer questions
sections.explanation: People need different answers at different moments. Match the next piece of information to the question they are actually asking.

items.label: Awareness
items.detail: What is this, and why should I care?

items.label: Consideration
items.detail: Is this right for me? Show comparisons and proof.

items.label: Conversion
items.detail: Can I act safely and easily?

items.label: Retention
items.detail: Did the experience deliver on the promise?

items.label: Advocacy
items.detail: Is this worth recommending to someone else?

sections.takeaway: Real journeys loop and pause. This sequence is a planning model, not a rule about human behaviour.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. The journey is a series of customer questions

sections.title: A thousand visits is not a thousand customers
sections.explanation: The lesson’s example becomes 30 enquiries, 12 qualified prospects and 3 customers. Each rate applies to the previous stage, not to all visitors.

items.label: Visitors
items.detail: People entering the example funnel.

items.label: Enquiries
items.detail: 3% of visitors make an enquiry.

items.label: Qualified prospects
items.detail: 40% of enquiries meet the qualification rule.

items.label: Customers
items.detail: 25% of qualified prospects buy.

sections.takeaway: Overall conversion is 3 ÷ 1,000 = 0.3%. Compare acquisition cost with contribution margin and realistic customer value, not revenue alone.
sections.caption: Synthetic worked example matching the reading: 1,000 × 3% × 40% × 25% = 3. Funnel widths are schematic, not proportional. The adjustable ₹3,000 budget is an added practice assumption.

sections.title: Diagnose the leak before adding traffic
sections.explanation: Choose the fix that matches the stage losing people. More visitors do not solve a form that nobody can finish.

items.label: Attention leak
items.detail: Wrong audience or weak hook → revisit research and the promise.

items.label: Trust leak
items.detail: Unanswered questions → add proof, comparisons and useful content.

items.label: Action leak
items.detail: Slow page or long form → remove friction and show the full offer.

items.label: Relationship leak
items.detail: Silence after purchase → onboard, support and follow up with permission.

sections.takeaway: Measure a stage rate before and after a change so you can tell whether the fix helped.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. Why funnels leak — and the patch for each hole

sections.title: Match the channel to the moment
sections.explanation: A channel’s role depends on the customer question. Do not ask a discovery campaign to behave like a high-intent search.

items.label: Discover
items.detail: Social, video and relevant creator content introduce the problem.

items.label: Evaluate
items.detail: Search guides, reviews and comparison content build confidence.

items.label: Act
items.detail: A relevant landing page and clear follow-up support the decision.

items.label: Return / recommend
items.detail: Permission-based email and community support the relationship.

sections.takeaway: Channel hand-offs matter: the promise on the ad should survive the click onto the page.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: If the enquiry rate doubles and all other rates stay fixed, what happens to expected customers?
checkpoint.answer: They double from 3 to 6. With the same media spend, CPA halves. That is a forecast under fixed assumptions, not proof that a real campaign will behave that way.

m1-t3.introduction: Turn scattered reviews, searches and conversations into an evidence-backed audience picture. Keep the difference between an observation and a guess visible.

sections.title: Climb the evidence ladder
sections.explanation: Research gets stronger when you record what people actually say and do, rather than inventing a perfect customer.

items.label: Observe
items.detail: Collect repeated phrases from reviews, searches and interviews.

items.label: Tag
items.detail: Mark needs, barriers, situations and buying triggers.

items.label: Check
items.detail: Compare signals across more than one source.

items.label: Decide
items.detail: Choose a message or channel and name the evidence behind it.

sections.takeaway: A single interview suggests a hypothesis; it does not represent the entire market.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: A persona is a decision tool
sections.explanation: Useful personas explain the situation in which someone buys. Decorative demographics cannot tell you what to say next.

items.label: Need
items.detail: What job is the customer trying to get done?

items.label: Trigger
items.detail: Why look for a solution now?

items.label: Barrier
items.detail: What could stop a purchase or enquiry?

items.label: Proof
items.detail: What would make the promise believable?

sections.takeaway: Link each persona claim to a source or label it as an assumption to test.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Find a gap, not a brand to copy
sections.explanation: A competitor teardown asks where customer needs remain unanswered. The useful output is an opportunity, not a list of features.

items.label: Compare
items.detail: Review offers, search visibility, content and customer feedback.

items.label: Spot the gap
items.detail: Notice repeated questions, complaints or missing information.

items.label: Choose a response
items.detail: Offer clearer proof, a simpler next step or a relevant explanation.

sections.takeaway: Copying a rival’s post does not copy the research, distribution or brand trust behind it.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. Competitor teardown: hunt for gaps, not features

sections.title: A small research desk
sections.explanation: Free tools contribute different types of evidence. Use them together and keep dates and source links.

items.label: Search evidence
items.detail: Autocomplete and trends suggest language and changing interest.

items.label: Review evidence
items.detail: Reviews reveal recurring praise, frustration and missing answers.

items.label: Human evidence
items.detail: Short interviews explain context that dashboards cannot.

items.label: Competitor evidence
items.detail: Public pages show positioning, offers and content gaps.

sections.takeaway: Search interest is not sales volume. Tool estimates and convenience samples have limits.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: A review says “I could not find the fee.” What is the research-to-action chain?
checkpoint.answer: Record the quote and source, look for the same barrier elsewhere, then test a clear fee section or enquiry answer. Do not assume one review proves every prospect has that barrier.

sections.section: 4. Where the evidence lives — a free toolkit

m1-t4.introduction: Connect the business goal to the numbers you can act on. Finish with a one-page brief that a teammate could use without guessing.

sections.title: Write a target people can check
sections.explanation: A useful goal specifies an outcome, a baseline, a target and a time window. The target below is a practice goal, not a forecast.

items.label: Baseline
items.detail: Current monthly count, using a fixed qualification definition.

items.label: Target
items.detail: Practice target for the end of the next eight weeks.

sections.takeaway: Moving from 20 to 30 is a 50% increase. Whether it is achievable needs evidence about demand, capacity and budget.
sections.caption: Synthetic worked example, not live campaign data or an industry benchmark.
sections.section: 1. SMART goals: the sentence that ends arguments

sections.title: From the goal to the diagnostic levers
sections.explanation: The KPI tree separates the business outcome from the numbers that explain why it moved.

items.label: Demand
items.detail: Relevant visits and enquiries indicate available interest.

items.label: Lead quality
items.detail: Qualified enquiries show whether the right people arrived.

items.label: Conversion
items.detail: Counselling-to-admission rate reveals decision-stage performance.

items.label: Cost guardrail
items.detail: CPA shows whether the acquisition plan is affordable.

sections.takeaway: Keep metric definitions and time windows consistent from the top of the tree to its branches.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. The KPI tree: how a goal becomes daily numbers

sections.title: Budget logic you can defend
sections.explanation: Work backwards from the goal before choosing activity. An assumed rate belongs in the plan as an assumption.

items.label: Business goal
items.detail: Name the number of new customers or admissions needed.

items.label: Required leads
items.detail: Divide the target by an evidence-backed close-rate assumption.

items.label: Required traffic
items.detail: Divide leads by the assumed visit-to-lead rate.

items.label: Budget verdict
items.detail: Estimate spend and compare CPA with a margin-aware ceiling.

sections.takeaway: Distinguish a KPI that judges success from a diagnostic metric that helps explain it.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. Goal → KPI → metric: the budget logic

sections.title: The one-page operating contract
sections.explanation: A brief joins the why, who, what and how. It also records what the campaign will not attempt.

items.label: Direction
items.detail: Business goal, audience need and single message.

items.label: Execution
items.detail: Channel roles, assets, owner and dates.

items.label: Control
items.detail: Budget, KPI definitions, risk and pause rules.

items.label: Boundaries
items.detail: Out-of-scope work and untested assumptions.

sections.takeaway: The brief is the reference when a new idea competes for limited time or money.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Is “get more followers” a complete SMART campaign goal?
checkpoint.answer: No. State the business purpose, the defined baseline and numeric target, a realistic time window, and the outcome that follower growth is meant to support.
